hops.afterHeading: How do you follow a cell that leaves?
hops.title: Ducks with quail beaks, quail with duck bills
hops.text: In 2003, Richard Schneider and Jill Helms swapped cranial neural crest between two birds with very different faces: quail, with short pointed beaks, and ducks, with broad flat bills. Duck hosts grew stubby quail beaks, and quail hosts grew flat duck bills; the lab later nicknamed the chimeras qucks and duails. The odd part is the egg tooth, the small bump a hatchling uses to crack its shell. It grows entirely from host skin, not crest. Yet duck skin built an egg tooth like a quail's conical one, and quail skin built one like a duck's flat nail. The crest cells were giving orders to their neighbors.

sources.citation: Schneider RA, Helms JA. The cellular and molecular origins of beak morphology. Science. 2003;299(5606):565-568.
Schneider RA. Neural crest and the origin of species-specific pattern. Genesis. 2018;56(6-7):e23219.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A speckled brown quail chick with a broad yellow duck bill sitting beside a yellow duckling with a short pointed quail beak.
image.caption: Swapped cranial crest gives each bird the other species' beak, and even reshapes the host's egg tooth.

hops.afterHeading: Steering: a forbidden half and cells that back away
hops.title: An X-linked syndrome that hits females harder
hops.text: Craniofrontonasal syndrome comes from loss-of-function mutations in EFNB1, the X-linked gene for ephrin-B1, and its severity runs in a direction geneticists call paradoxical. Males with no working ephrin-B1 at all usually have only wide-set eyes. Females with one working copy often have fused skull seams and marked changes to the face. Random X-inactivation makes the female head a patchwork of cells with and without ephrin-B1, and the leading explanation is that the two kinds sort apart at their borders. The test came from six males with the severe, female-like form: all six turned out to be mosaics, with an estimated 15 to 69 percent mutant cells in the samples tested.

sources.citation: Twigg SR, Babbs C, van den Elzen ME, et al. Cellular interference in craniofrontonasal syndrome: males mosaic for mutations in the X-linked EFNB1 gene are more severely affected than true hemizygotes. Hum Mol Genet. 2013;22(8):1654-1662.

Niethamer TK, Teng T, Franco M, Du YX, Percival CJ, Bush JO. Aberrant cell segregation in the craniofacial primordium and the emergence of facial dysmorphology in craniofrontonasal syndrome. PLoS Genet. 2020;16(2):e1008300.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two quilts on a wooden table: a smooth solid blue quilt beside a quilt whose blue and terracotta squares form uneven clusters with curving, puckered seams where they meet.
image.caption: A patchwork of ephrin-B1 cells does more harm than losing ephrin-B1 everywhere.

hops.afterHeading: Neurocristopathies: tissues that fail together often share a requirement
hops.title: Why blue-eyed white cats are often deaf, and why albinism is not the reason
hops.text: White cats with blue eyes are often deaf, but albinism is not why. True albino cats carry a tyrosinase mutation and make no melanin, yet they can hear, because crest-derived melanocytes still reach the inner ear. Dominant white cats instead carry a feline endogenous retrovirus fragment in KIT, and an affected cochlea can lack melanocytes. In most Kit-mutant mice studied, those cells were missing and the electrical potential hearing needs stayed near zero. In two mixed-breed research colonies, 65 and 85 percent of white cats with two blue eyes were deaf in one or both ears.

sources.citation: David VA, Menotti-Raymond M, Wallace AC, et al. Endogenous retrovirus insertion in the KIT oncogene determines white and white spotting in domestic cats. G3 (Bethesda). 2014;4(10):1881-1891.
Strain GM. The Genetics of Deafness in Domestic Animals. Front Vet Sci. 2015;2:29.
Steel KP, Barkway C. Another role for melanocytes: their importance for normal stria vascularis development in the mammalian inner ear. Development. 1989;107(3):453-463.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two white cats on a sunny windowsill near a brass bell: a pink-eyed albino cat turns its ears toward the bell while a blue-eyed white cat watches a butterfly.
image.caption: Albino cats keep inner-ear melanocytes and hear; in dominant white cats, loss of cochlear melanocytes can cause deafness.
